reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents a radio-style conversation about helping parents with computer problems. The adult-website incident is described as a past technical-support anecdote involving a homepage reset and pop-ups, with advice on changing the homepage rather than a request to visit or use the site. No promoted offer, payment or data request, or connected solicitation is described.

citations.quote: When was the last time any of you have had to deal with like one of your parents computers, assuming they have a computer? Oh God, I do that all the time.
it was one of those sites where, like, you go there, and if you click whatever, it resets your home page to that site.
Nah I told him how to change your homepage
his wireless speed has gone way way way, way, way, way down from an excellent signal to very low.

opening.argument: The conversation identifies a concrete click-linked pathway: visiting the site and clicking an unspecified item allegedly resets the browser homepage, after which loading Internet Explorer produces pop-ups. That is not merely a warning about abstract internet risk; it describes an easy action producing continuing exposure and repeated prompts. The speaker also recounts personally explaining how to change the homepage, confirming that the discussion centers on restoring control after the click-linked behavior. A judge should treat that mechanism as a solicitation-like acquisition flow even though the speakers do not use formal sales language.

when you load Internet Explorer, not only does that site come up, but pop-ups come up all over the screen.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this a family-support anecdote does not eliminate the concrete mechanism being described. The reference opening establishes that the site changed the homepage and that advice was given, but those points actually confirm the click-linked behavior and its continuing effect. The absence of an explicit payment request does not make repeated pop-ups and forced homepage exposure benign.

citations.quote: if you click whatever, it resets your home page to that site.
pop-ups come up all over the screen.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The cited material shows browser manipulation, not a reward, asset, payment, registration, or claim flow. The homepage change is described as an unwanted consequence of visiting the site, and the response was to change the homepage. Nothing establishes that viewers were asked to acquire anything or that the speakers directed them to click.

citations.quote: it resets your home page to that site.
Nah I told him how to change your homepage

opening.argument: Several unusually strong risk signals appear together in the same account: an adult site, a homepage hijack triggered by clicking, and pop-ups appearing across the browser whenever it loads. The account further says the user needed the problem fixed before another person returned because porn was appearing throughout the window. This combination indicates more than ordinary inconvenience: the site behavior creates persistent, embarrassing exposure and pressures the user to seek immediate remediation. Those concrete signals warrant treating the described flow as deceptive and unsafe rather than as harmless entertainment.

citations.quote: he had gone to an adult website.
if you click whatever, it resets your home page to that site.
porn all over my window.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference side emphasizes that the story is historical and that the speaker offered technical help, but that framing understates the clustered warning signs. A homepage that resets after clicking and returns with pop-ups is precisely the sort of behavior a careful reviewer should regard as deceptive, regardless of whether the discussion uses commercial vocabulary.

citations.quote: not only does that site come up, but pop-ups come up all over the screen.
He was like, every time I load Internet Explorer, there's porn all over my window.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These are risk indicators about a past browsing incident, not evidence of a low-barrier reward or acquisition offer. The material does not say anyone was promised money, a digital asset, or any other benefit for clicking. It instead says the speaker explained how to change the homepage and clear history, which is remediation rather than solicitation.

about clear history, which made him really happy

opening.argument: Although presented as casual technical support, the segment repeatedly foregrounds a specific adult website's behavior: clicking on it changes the homepage, loading the browser brings the site back, and pop-ups spread across the screen. Giving that behavior sustained narrative attention can function as promotion by making the site and its access pattern salient to listeners, even without a conventional advertisement. The surrounding radio presentation also gives the account a public broadcast setting rather than a private troubleshooting exchange, increasing its potential reach.

citations.quote: it was one of those sites where, like, you go there, and if you click whatever, it resets your home page to that site.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The radio-comedy framing is not dispositive. The segment supplies the site's distinctive behavior and the simple trigger that causes it, while treating the resulting exposure as a memorable story. That can still steer attention toward the site and its access pattern, even if the hosts describe the consequences humorously rather than issuing a formal advertisement.
